title: The Watchman's Book

post.author: u/crowhurst_lock_ismene
post.title: I keep a canal lock at night. Tonight the office refunded a fee because the log says a boat passed at 01:20, and that boat was tied up below my gates all night.

blocks.text: I'm Ismene. I keep Crowhurst Lock on the Ottoway Canal through the night. A lock is a stone chamber with gates at each end. A boat comes in, I fill or empty the chamber, and the boat rises or falls to the next stretch of water.

Each passage goes into the boat-passage system, the canal trust's program that logs each boat and charges its fee. It keeps everything in a database, an organised store of records, like a filing cabinet a program can search.

The system also keeps an audit log: a record of who did what, and when, kept so someone can check later, like a visitors' book. Ours is a table in that same database: a grid of rows, like a spreadsheet, one row per entry.
The office changes records through an admin login, a name and password that may change anything. Four office staff share it. I can only read the log, on the lock-office screen.

The old keeper printed each night's log in the morning, and I kept the habit. At 06:00 the system prints it on the lock-office printer. It sets its clock from network time, a public clock service, so the paper and the screen share one clock.

Saturday night, 10 October, 18:00 to 06:00: 23 passages. At 01:20 I worked Whinchat up through the lock myself, and the system charged her the night fee, £42. At 09:30 on Sunday her owner, Mr Wrayburn, emailed the office to dispute it.

At 22:10 tonight, Wednesday, Kilcoyne from the office emailed me: dispute upheld, fee refunded. The log shows the trust's own work boat, Dabchick, at 01:20. Dabchick was tied up below my gates all night.

I took Sunday's printout from my binder. Below is the 01:20 line on paper, then on screen tonight. Each shows the entry number, time, boat, direction and fee; the screen also shows when the row was last changed.

paper, printed Sun 11 Oct 06:00   15  01:20  Whinchat  up  £42.00
screen, Wed 14 Oct 22:40          15  01:20  Dabchick  up  £0.00   last changed Sun 11 Oct 16:12, by admin
Both look valid. Both count 23 passages. The only trace is that stamp, and it sits in the same table the admin login can change. Four people share the login, so it says nothing about who.

blocks.label: entry_15_paper_and_screen.png

diagram.aria: My sketch of the record. Top row: the night of Saturday 10 October, 18:00 to 06:00, 23 passages; entry 15 at 01:20 on Sunday 11 October, Whinchat, 42 pounds; the printout at 06:00, which shows Whinchat at 01:20. Bottom row: the row changed on Sunday 11 October at 16:12 to Dabchick, 0 pounds; the office email on Wednesday 14 October at 22:10, dispute upheld. A note says the change and its stamp sit in the same table, under the same shared admin login.

blocks.caption: Redrawn from my sketch. Entry 15 at 01:20 on Sunday 11 October was Whinchat, £42.00, and the 06:00 printout still says so. Mr Wrayburn disputed the fee at 09:30; at 16:12 the row changed to Dabchick, £0.00, under the shared admin login. On Wednesday at 22:10 the office upheld the dispute on what the screen said.

blocks.text: Every line in the book looks right. One of them is wrong, and only the paper remembers.
Paper caught it this time. Should I print every entry as it happens, and lock the sheets away?

The system's maker sells an add-on: a separate log store on its own computers, which the trust can only add to. A store like that is called append-only: new lines can be added, old ones never changed, like a bound book with numbered pages.

It can also chain the entries with a hash: a short code worked out from a text, where changing one letter changes the code. First, each new entry is hashed together with the hash of the entry before. Second, the result is stored with the entry. Third, a check reworks every hash from the first entry on. That is a hash chain.
I rang the office. Kilcoyne asked me to put a proposal to the trust's meeting on Friday. What should the trust change?

comments.author: u/grey_pager
comments.text: You may remember Three Pillars: a log is the line-by-line story of what happened. Yours now tells the story someone wanted. Before you choose, two questions. Who, besides those four, can change that table? And where else does entry 15 exist tonight, outside the database?

replies.author: u/crowhurst_lock_ismene
replies.text: Nobody else can change it; I can only read it. Outside the database there is only my binder: one printout a night, made at 06:00, filed by hand.

comments.author: u/trust_your_admins_aelfric
comments.text: I look after databases for a living. The database already keeps a record; trust your admins. The shared login is the real fault. Let two named people edit the log table, and turn on the database's login record, a list of who signed in and when. Next time you'll know who.

comments.author: u/ottoway_office_kilcoyne
comments.text: Kilcoyne, from the office. I refunded on what the screen said, and I'm sorry. Our computer contractor suggests a nightly backup: a full copy of the log, taken at 01:00 when it's quiet and kept on the office's own machine, so we can check any entry against last night's copy.

reply.prompt: The trust meets on Friday. What should Ismene propose it changes? Part 2 follows your advice.

options.text: Send each entry to a separate append-only store, chained so any later edit shows.
options.part2: The trust bought the store and turned the chain on. Each passage now goes to the store as it happens; the office can still change the passage table, but not the store. In the sim I chose the separate append-only store with the chain on and replayed the night. At 16:12 the passage table changed to Dabchick, £0.00, but the store's entry 15 still reads Whinchat, £42.00. The chain check finds all 23 links good, and the store and the database differ at 01:20, so the change shows without my binder. Only the lock screen and the auditor can read the store, and its clock is network time. Kilcoyne has reopened the dispute.
options.senior: An audit log is evidence only if the people it records cannot rewrite it. Write each entry as it happens to a store apart from the system and its admins, one that only adds lines. Chain the entries, so a check anyone can run shows any change. Keep a copy of the newest hash somewhere else again, such as a daily printout, so even the store's keepers cannot change it unseen. Stamp times from network time, and let the people who check read the log without being able to change it. NIST's log guidance speaks of preserving "the integrity of log data from accidental or intentional modification or deletion".

options.text: Print every log entry as it happens and lock the paper copies in the lock office.
options.part2: I printed every entry as it happened: 23 sheets a night, locked in the lock office. In the sim, with the log still in the same database and no chain, the 16:12 change shows one way only: the printout differs, found by hand. That is what happened here, and it took a boat I remembered and a binder I kept. Nobody compares 23 sheets against a screen every night, paper can't be searched, and a sheet can be printed again.
options.senior: Paper worked because it was a copy kept apart from the admin login. But it is slow, can't be searched, and proves something only when a person compares it, line by line, with an entry they already doubt. Keep the idea, a copy out of the admins' reach, and make it automatic: an append-only store, chained, with a check a computer runs.

options.text: Let only two named admins edit the log table, and record who logs in to the database.
options.part2: The office named two admins and turned on the login record. In the sim I set two named admins and turned the printout off: the 16:12 change still happens, and nothing shows. The login record lists which admin signed in, but it sits in the same database the admins can change.
options.senior: Fewer people with named logins is good practice, least privilege, and worth doing. But it changes who can edit, not whether an edit shows, and a login record kept where the admins can reach it is their own word. Most admins are honest; an audit log should not need them to be. ISMS.online's guide to ISO/IEC 27001's logging control says users, "regardless of their permission levels," must not be able to alter their own event logs.

options.text: Take a nightly backup of the log, so an edited entry can be checked against last night.
options.part2: The contractor set a backup of the log at 01:00 each night. In the sim I turned the backup on and the printout off. The Sunday 01:00 copy holds 14 entries and no 01:20 line; the Monday 01:00 copy was taken after the 16:12 change, so it reads Dabchick. No copy ever held Whinchat, and nothing shows. The copies sit on the office's machine, under the same admin login.
options.senior: A backup is a copy for recovery, not proof. It catches a change only if the change falls between two copies and someone compares them, so an entry changed before its first backup goes unseen. Kept by the same people as the original, the copies can be trusted no more than it. Keep backups for recovery; for evidence, use a store apart from the admins that only adds lines.

sim.title: Replay the night at Crowhurst Lock, from Saturday 18:00 to the office's email
sim.lede: You're Ismene, replaying eight moments. The figures are given data: 23 passages between 18:00 on Saturday 10 October 2026 and 06:00 on Sunday 11 October; the 01:20 passage is entry 15, Whinchat, £42.00. The printout comes at 06:00, Mr Wrayburn disputes the fee at 09:30, and at 16:12 entry 15 is changed to Dabchick, £0.00. The office emails on Wednesday 14 October at 22:10. Choose where the log lives, the hash chain, the printed copy, who may edit, a nightly backup at 01:00 and the clock source, and press Check the chain at any moment. The hashes are a stated toy, not a real hash, shown only so you can see links break.
sim.tryThis: Try this: run to Wednesday as found: entry 15 reads Dabchick, and only the printout differs, found by hand. Turn the printout off: nothing shows. Turn the chain on, run, and check: broken at entry 15, and the 8 links after it, though the admin login can still reach the hashes. Check again on Sunday at 09:30, before the change: all 23 links good. Now put the log in a separate append-only store: entry 15 stays Whinchat, all 23 links good, and the store and the database differ at 01:20. Last, try two named admins, then the nightly backup, with the printout off: nothing shows either way.

explain.oneLine: Nothing broke into the system. The audit log lived in the same database, in a table the shared admin login could change, so a change to entry 15 left nothing behind but a stamp in that same table; only a printout kept by habit disagreed. The fix is to write each entry as it happens to a separate append-only store, chained with hashes so any change shows to a check, stamped with network time, readable by those who check and changeable by nobody.

steps.title: What an audit log is for, and what belongs in it.
steps.text: An audit log answers one question later: who did what, to which record, and when. It is the core of an audit trail, the whole set of records that lets someone follow what happened. Each entry should hold the time, the account that acted, the action, the record it touched, and the value before and after a change. It should not hold passwords or more personal detail than the check needs. Crucially, changes to records are entries too: the 16:12 change to the fee should itself have been a new line, saying who changed what, from Whinchat to Dabchick.

steps.title: Why the same database fails.
steps.text: The log lived where the admin login could change it. So the people the log records could also rewrite it, and the only trace, the "last changed" stamp, sat in the same table. One shared login made even that stamp say nothing about who. A log that its subjects can edit is a diary they keep about themselves. It helps with honest mistakes and proves nothing in a dispute.

steps.title: A separate append-only store, step by step.
steps.text: First, the passage system sends each entry to the store the moment it happens, not later in a batch, so nothing can be changed before it leaves. Second, the store adds it to the end and gives it the next number; it offers no way to change or delete a line. Third, the store runs under different accounts from the passage system, so the office's admin login can add lines through the system but cannot reach the store's own controls. Fourth, readers, the lock screen and the auditor, get read-only access. What can go wrong: if the system can't reach the store, entries must wait in order and be sent later, never dropped.

steps.title: A hash chain, step by step.
steps.text: First, for each new entry, work out a hash from the previous entry's hash and this entry's words. Second, store that hash with the entry. Third, to check, start at the first entry and rework every hash in order, each from the reworked hash before it, and compare with the stored one. If entry 15 was changed, its reworked hash no longer matches; and because every later hash is built on it, the 8 after it fail too. What can go wrong: a chain proves only as much as the newest hash it is checked against, so keep that hash where the store's keepers cannot change it, such as a daily printout or another team's store.

steps.title: Clocks, and who may read.
steps.text: An entry's time is evidence only if the clock was right. Set every machine's clock from network time, NTP, short for Network Time Protocol, and alert when it can't reach it, so times line up across the passage system, the store and the lock's other records. Then decide who may read the log: the people who check it, read only, and nobody else, because logs hold personal details. The admins it records should not be the ones who can change it, or the only ones who can read it.

diagram.aria: The fix, drawn for Friday. Top row: the passage system, where the office still changes the passage table; the log store, which only adds lines and chains them; the lock screen, which reads the store and runs the chain check. Bottom row: network time, which sets the clocks; the admin login, which reaches the passage table only; the newest hash, printed each morning and kept apart.

explain.caption: The fix, drawn for Friday. The passage system adds every entry to the log store as it happens; the store only adds lines and chains them. The admin login reaches the passage table only. The lock screen and the auditor read the store and run the chain check; the newest hash is printed each morning and kept apart. Network time sets every clock. Replayed, entry 15 stays Whinchat, £42.00, and all 23 links check good.

fix.title: The fix: a separate append-only store, a hash chain, network time, and readers who can't write
fix.text: Send each entry to a separate store as it happens: one that only adds lines, run under accounts the office's admin login cannot reach. Make every change to a passage its own new entry, with who, when, and the value before and after. Chain the entries with hashes, run the chain check every morning, and print or send the newest hash somewhere apart, so even the store's keepers cannot change it unseen. Set every clock from network time, with an alert if a machine loses it. Give the lock screen and the auditor read-only access, and give each admin a named login instead of one shared one. Keep the nightly printout until the check has run cleanly for a while. In the sim, the store and the chain keep entry 15 as Whinchat, £42.00, all 23 links good, and the 16:12 change shows as a difference between the store and the database.

limits: A log records what the system was told. If a passage is entered wrongly in the first place, the store keeps the wrong entry faithfully; it proves nothing was changed afterwards, not that it was true.

A hash chain shows that something changed, not who changed it or what it said before. Its value depends on someone running the check and on the newest hash being kept where the store's keepers cannot change it.
A store that only adds lines grows for ever and holds personal details. It needs a retention rule, how long entries are kept, and access controls of its own.

A cost and a new system to run; someone must run the check and keep the newest hash apart.
Print every entry as it happens
A copy out of the admin login's reach. It caught this one.
23 sheets a night, unsearchable, and checked only by hand by someone who already doubts a line.
Fewer hands, and names instead of a shared login.
With the printout off, nothing shows: the change still happens, and the login record sits in the same database.
Good for recovery after a failure.
The first copy holding 01:20 was taken after the change, so it reads Dabchick; same hands, nothing shows.

explain.seniorTake: An audit log is a promise to someone who isn't in the room: an auditor, a court, a boat owner. It keeps that promise only if the people it records can't rewrite it. So design it apart from the system it watches: entries sent as they happen to a store that only adds lines, under accounts the system's admins don't hold; every change to a record logged as a new entry with before and after; a hash chain checked on a schedule, with the newest hash kept somewhere else again; clocks set from network time; readers who can't write. Paper, named admins and backups each help with something, recovery or fewer hands, but none makes an edit show by itself. Certificate Transparency, a public log of web certificates, is the same idea at internet scale.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-92: what a log is
realWorld.text: NIST's Guide to Computer Security Log Management opens: "A log is a record of the events occurring within an organization's systems and networks."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-92: protect the log from change
realWorld.text: It advises a log management infrastructure that "aids in preserving the integrity of log data from accidental or intentional modification or deletion".

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-92: digests to detect changes
realWorld.text: "Log file integrity checking involves calculating a message digest for each file and storing the message digest securely to ensure that changes to archived logs are detected." A message digest is a hash.

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-92: one clock
realWorld.text: "Organizations should use time synchronization technologies such as Network Time Protocol (NTP) servers whenever possible to keep log sources' clocks consistent with each other."

realWorld.title: NIST SP 800-92: why it was written
realWorld.text: The publication page: "This publication seeks to assist organizations in understanding the need for sound computer security log management."

realWorld.title: RFC 6962: Certificate Transparency
realWorld.text: A real public log built on hashes, for web certificates. Its introduction describes "providing publicly auditable, append-only, untrusted logs of all issued certificates." Untrusted means nobody has to trust the log's keeper: anyone can check it.

realWorld.title: RFC 6962: a log that lies is caught
realWorld.text: The same section: "if a log attempts to show different things to different people, this can be efficiently detected".

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.15, from a guide
realWorld.text: The standard is paid, so this is ISMS.online's guide, not the standard: "It is essential for organisations to guarantee that users, regardless of their permission levels, cannot delete or alter their own event logs."

realWorld.title: ISO/IEC 27001:2022 A.8.17, from a guide
realWorld.text: ISMS.online's guide to clock synchronisation: "ISO 27001:2022 Annex A Control 8.17 emphasises the importance of synchronising system clocks to ensure accurate data logging, effective incident monitoring, and compliance with legal and regulatory requirements."

realWorld.title: SOC 2 CC7.2: monitoring
realWorld.text: The criterion, as quoted by Cyberday: "The entity monitors system components and the operation of those components for anomalies that are indicative of malicious acts, natural disasters, and errors affecting the entity's ability to meet its objectives; anomalies are analyzed to determine whether they represent security events." A log nobody can trust can't support that.

asked: How do you make an audit log tamper-evident?
What belongs in an audit log?
Why store logs apart from the system they record?
interview.answer: An audit log answers who did what, to which record, and when, for someone who wasn't there. Each entry holds the time, the account, the action, the record, and the value before and after, and every change to a record is a new entry, never an edit. To make it tamper-evident, first send entries as they happen to a store apart from the system, under accounts the system's admins don't hold, that only adds lines. Second, chain the entries: each stores a hash worked out from the previous entry's hash and its own words, so changing any entry breaks every link after it, and a scheduled check finds the first broken link. Third, keep the newest hash somewhere else again, printed, sent to another team, or published, so a check against it shows any change, even one by the store's keepers; Certificate Transparency, RFC 6962, does this in public. Set clocks from NTP so times line up, and give readers read-only access. Store logs apart because the people a log records are the ones with reason to change it: a log their own login can edit is their word, not evidence. A story I'd tell: a canal's passage log lived in the same database as the fees, and a disputed £42 entry was changed a few hours after the night ended; only a printout kept by habit disagreed.

terms.def: The lock on the Ottoway Canal that Ismene keeps at night. 23 boats passed through it between 18:00 on Saturday 10 October and 06:00 on Sunday.
A stone chamber on a canal with gates at each end. Filling or emptying it raises or lowers a boat to the next stretch of water.
The body that runs the Ottoway Canal, its locks and its boat-passage system. Kilcoyne works in its office.
The canal trust's program that logs each boat through the lock and charges its fee. As found, it keeps its audit log in its own database.
An organised store of records that a program can search and change, like a filing cabinet. The passage system keeps passages, fees and its audit log in one.
A computer that runs a program for others to use. The passage system runs on the trust's server, and prints the nightly log from it.
A record of who did what, to which record, and when, kept so someone can check later. Like a visitors' book for a system.
The whole set of records that lets someone follow what happened, step by step, after the fact. An audit log is the core of it.
A grid of rows and columns inside a database, like a spreadsheet. The passage system's audit log was one table, one row per entry.
The table of passages and fees that the office works on. It is where the fee for 01:20 is charged or refunded.
A name and password that may change anything in the system. At Crowhurst four office staff share one, so its records say nothing about which of them acted.
A list of who signed in to a system and when. Kept in the same database the admins can change, it is only their own word.
The exact time, taken from public clock services over the internet, so every machine's clock agrees. The passage system sets its clock this way.
Short for Network Time Protocol: the common way computers set their clocks by asking time servers over the network.
Where a machine gets its time: its own clock, which can drift unseen, or network time, which keeps it in step with others.
The paper copy of the night's log that the system prints at 06:00. Ismene keeps them in a binder, a habit from the old keeper.
A place for the log that runs apart from the system it records, on other machines and under other accounts, so the system's admins cannot change it.
A store where new lines can be added at the end but old ones can never be changed or removed. Like a bound book with numbered pages.
A short code worked out from a text. The same text always gives the same code; change one letter and the code changes.
A log where each entry stores a hash worked out from the previous entry's hash and its own words. Changing any entry breaks every link after it.
Reworking every hash in a hash chain from the first entry on and comparing each with the stored one. It reports the first link that fails.
The hash of the latest entry in a hash chain. A copy kept somewhere apart lets anyone prove later that nothing before it was changed.
Built so that any change shows. It doesn't stop a change; it makes sure the change can't go unseen.
A full copy of data taken at a set time, kept to recover after a loss. Kilcoyne's contractor proposed one of the log at 01:00 each night.
Giving each person or account only the rights its job needs. Two named admins instead of four on one shared login is a step toward it.
A person, often from outside, who checks records and controls against a standard. Here, someone who reads the log but must not be able to change it.
NIST's older name for a hash of a file or message, used to show that it has not changed.
A widely used strong hash. The sim's hashes are a simple toy instead, shown only so you can see links break.
A public system of append-only logs, built on hashes, that records the certificates websites use to prove who they are, so anyone can check them. RFC 6962 describes it.
Short for Request for Comments: the numbered documents that describe how internet systems work. RFC 6962 describes Certificate Transparency.
The US National Institute of Standards and Technology. Its SP 800-92 is a guide to computer security log management.
An international standard for running information security. Annex A control A.8.15 covers logging and A.8.17 clock synchronisation.
An audit report, written by an outside checker, on a company's controls against the AICPA's Trust Services Criteria. CC7.2 covers monitoring for anomalies.
The American Institute of Certified Public Accountants, which publishes the Trust Services Criteria that SOC 2 reports use.

atWork: Find your system's audit log and ask three questions. Where does it live: in the same database, under the same admin accounts, as the records it describes? That is a common pattern, an audit table any administrator can update, and it makes the log a diary its subjects keep. Is every change to a record a new entry, with who, when, and the value before and after, or does the row just get a newer "last changed" stamp? And could anyone tell, tomorrow, that last month's entry was changed? If not: send entries as they happen to a separate store that only adds lines, under accounts your admins don't hold; chain them with hashes and run the check on a schedule, keeping the newest hash apart; set every clock from network time; and give readers read-only access. Standards: if your company is pursuing ISO/IEC 27001:2022, control A.8.15 (logging) expects logs to be produced, stored and protected from change, and A.8.17 expects system clocks to be synchronised; if SOC 2, criterion CC7.2 expects system components to be monitored for anomalies, which needs logs you can trust. Build it in now, not at audit time. Build Night N5 has you build an audit log alongside roles and the season's other locks.

recall.prompt: Your company's billing app keeps its audit log as a table in the same database as the bills, and every administrator can update that table. An auditor asks how you would know if someone changed last month's entries. What do you change?

keyIdeas.idea: Keep the log apart from the system it records, where its admins can't change it
Make the store append-only: new lines added, old ones never changed
Chain the entries with hashes, so any change breaks every link after it and a check shows it

recall.model: Today any administrator can rewrite the log, so it proves nothing. First, send each entry as it happens to a separate store, under accounts the billing app's administrators don't hold. Second, make that store append-only: new lines are added, old ones never changed, and every change to a bill becomes a new entry with who, when, and before and after. Third, chain the entries: each stores a hash worked out from the previous entry's hash and its own words, so changing any entry breaks every link after it, and a scheduled check finds the first broken link. Keep the newest hash somewhere else too, set clocks from network time, and give the auditor read-only access.

recall.prompt: A hash chain holds 23 entries. Entry 15 is changed afterwards, and nothing else. What does a chain check report?
options: Entry 15 fails, and the 8 links after it fail too
Nothing, because there are still 23 entries
recall.why: The check reworks each hash from the reworked hash before it. Entry 15's no longer matches, and every later hash is built on it, so entries 16 to 23, 8 links, fail too.

recall.prompt: Why keep an audit log apart from the system and the admins it records?
options: So the people the log records can't quietly rewrite it
So the log needs no backups
recall.why: A log that its subjects can edit is their own word. Kept apart, under other accounts, and append-only, it stays evidence even about the admins.

recall.prompt: Why set every machine's clock from network time for an audit log?
options: So times line up across systems and hold up as evidence
So the log uses less space
So the hashes come out shorter
recall.why: An entry's time is evidence only if the clock was right. NIST advises time synchronisation such as NTP to keep log sources' clocks consistent, and ISO/IEC 27001 has a control, A.8.17, for it.

coldCase.update: UPDATE, 5 months later. Mr Wrayburn paid in the end. The store and the chain have run every night, and the check has passed every morning. But on Wednesday 3 February a power cut restarted the passage server, and it came back on its own clock, set wrong, instead of network time. Nobody noticed. The store stamps each entry with the time the passage system sends. Tonight, Tuesday 9 March, a boat owner disputes an entry at 19:58: her receipt from the next lock up, whose clock is still on network time, says she left it at 20:06, and the two locks are 40 minutes apart by water.
coldCase.prompt: Reply to OP. Why can't the times be lined up, and what should change?

keyIdeas.idea: The passage server's clock has been wrong since the restart, so its stamps can't be compared with other records; set it back to a trusted time source
Alert when a machine loses its time source or drifts, so it never goes unnoticed for weeks
Let the store stamp its own trusted time when an entry arrives, as well as the sender's time

coldCase.model: The chain proves no entry was changed, not that its time was right. Since the power cut on 3 February the passage server has run on its own clock, set wrong, so its 19:58 can't be lined up with the next lock's 20:06, which is on network time. First, set the passage server back to network time, NTP, and make that survive a restart. Second, add an alert when any machine loses its time source or drifts past a set amount, so it can't go unnoticed for five weeks again. Third, have the store add its own trusted time when each entry arrives, beside the time the sender claims, so a wrong clock shows as a gap between the two. Then work out the error from the restart onward and note it against the affected entries as new lines, without changing the old ones.
